{{Short description|American author}}{{use MDY dates|date=March 2020}}
'''Harold R. Jacobs''' (born 1939), who authored three mathematics books, both taught the subject and taught those who teach it.<ref name=MathBooksBy.A>{{cite web  |url=http://www.biblicalchristianworldview.net/documents/jacobsMath.pdf
   |title=The Mathematics textbooks authored by Harold R. Jacobs: An Analysis
   |author=James Nickel  |date=2004}}</ref> Since retiring he has continued writing articles, and as of 2012 had lectured "at more than 200" math conferences.

His books have been used by some [[Homeschooling|homeschoolers]]<ref name=HomeSchool.ElemAL2016>{{cite web
   |url=https://cathyduffyreviews.com/homeschool-reviews-core-curricula/math/math-grades-9-12/jacobs-elementary-algebra
   |title=Jacobs' Elementary Algebra
   |author=Cathy Duffy |date=September 5, 2018}}</ref> and has inspired followup works.

== Biography ==
Jacobs was born in [[North Hollywood]] and while in high school "realized that he wanted to become a teacher."<ref name="MathBooksBy.A" /> The 1939-born educator began "in the late 1960s" what became his first book, originally published in 1970, as an attempt  to address the needs of "those students who had not done well in mathematics."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://dimacs.rutgers.edu/Volumes/schools/paper82/node3.html|title=Mathematics, a Human Endeavor}}</ref> His works helped inspire other educators to extend areas such as "inquiry-based learning."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.artofmathematics.org/about/project-history|title=Art of Mathematics: Project History}}</ref> He chaired a high school math department in California for 12 years.<ref name="MathBooksBy.A" />

== Works ==

* (1970): ''Mathematics: A Human Endeavor'' (revised 1982, 1994) 
** A student workbook for this was subsequently written by Susan Knueven Wong.<ref name=MathBooksBy.A/>{{rp|p. 4}}<ref>{{cite book  
   |title=Student Workbook for Jacobs Mathematics: A Human Endeavor
   |author=Susan Knueven Wong  |isbn=978-071-672-539-8}}</ref>
** The 1994 edition was (re)titled as ''Mathematics, a Human Endeavor: A Textbook for Those Who Think They Don't Like the Subject''.<ref>{{cite book
   |url=https://www.thriftbooks.com/w/mathematics-a-human-endeavor-a-textbook-for-those-who-think-they-dont-like-the-subject_harold-r-jacobs/247083/#isbn=0716704390
   |title=Mathematics, a Human Endeavor: A Textbook for Those Who Think They Don't Like the Subject
   |isbn=071-67-0439-0 |author=Harold R. Jacobs}}</ref> Jacobs' approach, described as ahead of its time, was to introduce concepts<ref>{{cite web
   |url=https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/649958.Mathematics_a_Human_Endeavor
   |title=Mathematics, a Human Endeavor: A Book for Those Who Think They Don't Like the Subject}}</ref> in an entertaining yet practical way. Jacobs' description of the mathematics of ''[[Pool (cue sports)|billiards]]'' inspired a teacher to write a simulation in the [[Logo (programming language)|Logo educational computer programming language]] to help improve both his understanding and his teaching.<ref>{{cite web  |author=D. Burnett
   |url=http://people.uleth.ca/~d.burnett/2007Learning/Months/200701January/01Mathematics.htm
   |title=Learning: The Journey of a Lifetime  |date=January 2007}}</ref>

* (1974): ''Geometry: Seeing, Doing, Understanding'' (revised 1987, 2003). The 2003 edition makes reference to computer software such as ''[[The Geometer's Sketchpad]]''.<ref name=MathBooksBy.A/>{{rp|p. 3}} Even before this edition, the ''Teacher's notes'' for ''Geometry'' was used for developing new ways of teaching.<ref>{{cite web
   |url=http://www.meaningfulmath.org/numbers.pdf
   |title=Mathematical Modeling: Teaching the Open-ended Application of Mathematics
   |author=Joshua Paul Abrams
   |year=2001   |accessdate=March 2, 2020}}</ref><ref>Teacher's Guide: {{cite book
|url=https://www.thriftbooks.com/w/jacobs-geometry-solutions-manual_harold-r-jacobs/13549924/#isbn=1683440226&idiq=19811948
|title=Geometry (Teacher Guide) |author=Harold R. Jacobs
|isbn=9781683440222}}</ref> One instructor credited the book's success to being "mathematically very sound" yet using a "little by little" approach.<ref>{{cite web
   |url=https://www.mathmammoth.com/complete/harold_jacobs_geometry.php
   |title=Review of Harold Jacobs Geometry: Seeing, Doing, Understanding (third edition)
   |author=Maria Miller}}</ref>

* (1979): ''Elementary Algebra''<ref>{{cite book
   |title=Elementary Algebra  |url=https://archive.org/details/elementaryalgebr00jaco  |url-access=registration  |author=Harold R. Jacobs
   |isbn=9780716710479  |year=1979}}</ref><ref>Teacher's Guide: {{cite book
|title=Teacher's Guide to Elementary Algebra
|author=Harold R. Jacobs  
|isbn= 9780716710752}}</ref> (revised 2016)<ref name=HomeSchool.ElemAL2016/> The style of gently introducing new topics ahead of time, with details in a subsequent chapter, while accepted in homeschooling, has those who disagree for its use in classrooms.<ref>{{cite book
   |title=Elementary Algebra 0th Edition|isbn=0716710471}}</ref>

* several articles for Encyclopædia Britannica and The Mathematics Teacher.

The three books were published by [[W. H. Freeman and Company]], and "overhead transparencies for" classroom use were subsequently developed.<ref>{{cite web
   |url=http://www.exodusbooks.com/harold-jacobs-mathematics/2493
   |title=Harold Jacobs Mathematics
   |author=C. Hollis Crossman}}</ref> The ''Elementary Algebra'' text has attracted interest by homeschoolers, particularly when used in conjunction with an independently produced set of DVDs offering 36 hours of educational instruction.<ref name=HomeSchool.ElemAL2016/>
